newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia sets curbs to cool ringgit speculation.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia sets curbs to cool ringgit speculation.

text.p: Malaysia on Sunday announced curbs on local banks' activities in the foreign exchange market in a bid to cool speculation in the beleaguered ringgit.
The central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, said local banks would have to restrict their non-trade related swap transactions in the foreign exchange market to $2.0 million with each overseas customer.

"Banks are required with effect from 4 August 1997 to observe a limit of $2.0 million on outstanding non-commercial related ringgit offer side swap transactions with each foreign customer on a group basis," Bank Negara said in a statement.
Banks which have exceeded the limit will be forbidden further swap transactions until the outstandings are reduced, it said.
A swap is a forward rate agreement for exchanging one currency for another. The move means a foreigner involved in forward rate deals with Malaysian banks will have a ceiling of $2.0 million.
"Hedging requirements of foreigners for trade related and genuine portfolio and direct investments in Malaysia are not affected by this measure," the central bank said.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said last week that Malaysians were involved in the recent speculative attack on the ringgit by making available the local currency to speculators.
He hinted at possible action against speculators, without being specific.

"The move shouldn't surprise anyone, especially after Mahathir's warning," said Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at brokerage J.M. Sassoon & Co. "They had done that in the past, so why not do it this time around."
Malaysia imposed a similar restriction in February 1989.
"I guess they are quite obviously still unhappy with the level of the ringgit and the direction it is going," said an analyst with a Malaysian brokerage.

"Unfortunately, capital controls only work over the short term in general. If it is not just a speculative push but some underlying weakness in the currency, capital controls can only postpone the currency's slide."
Some analysts have not ruled out the possibility that more curbs will be introduced. They say Malaysia may impose negative interest rates on deposits placed by foreigners, as it did in 1994.
"That is the only effective way to get foreign fund managers with ringgit funds to move out," said a senior dealer with a large Malaysian bank.
Analysts and foreign exchange dealers said they expected a sell-off in dollar/ringgit on Monday and a jump in forward rates, following the swaps restriction.
"The first reaction is they are going to sell dollar/ringgit. It can easily fall 100 points," said the senior dealer.
Speculative attack on the ringgit over the past month has seen it fall more than five percent to a three-year low of 2.6530 per dollar. It closed at 2.6290/320 in Kuala Lumpur on Friday.

Bank Negara said its move was designed to help control interest rates more effectively. In the last two weeks, the central bank has been trying to lower rates in an attempt to boost domestic economic activity.
Analysts said the immediate impact on the stock market might be negative.

"It's good news for stocks in the longer term, maybe two weeks. But initial knee-jerk reaction will be negative as the market is averse to this kind of restrictive measures," said Faez Khairuddin, chief analyst at SJ Securities.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
